steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for our paper on using large language models to grade assignments in MOOCs as a replacement for peer grading. It should cover the motivation, our prompting approach, the models and courses we tested, the main findings, and a list of contributions.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
1. MOOCs, scale, and the grading problem; peer grading
2. NLP and LLMs as an opportunity; goal of this study
3. Our approach: prompting strategies, models, courses
4. Main findings
5. Contributions

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
1. MOOCs and grading
- MOOCs: free courses for anyone with internet; democratized, globally accessible, unlimited participants
- more participants -> hard to give personalized, constructive feedback, incl. grading assignments
- peer grading common practice; engagement + motivation, but reliability/validity questioned

2. NLP / LLMs
- from statistical methods to recent LLMs; NLP has fertilized other disciplines, enabled more complex tasks
- this study: can LLMs grade MOOC assignments, replace peer grading -> streamlined, automated grading
- less human intervention, more students served, more accurate feedback, better learning experience

3. Approach
- three prompting strategies, two LLMs: GPT-4, GPT-3.5
- three MOOC subjects: Introductory Astronomy, Astrobiology, History and Philosophy of Astronomy
- base: modified zero-shot chain-of-thought (Zero-shot-CoT), more in-context understanding of task
- (1) + instructor-provided answers; (2) + instructor answers and grading rubrics; (3) + instructor answers and LLM-generated rubrics

4. Findings
- GPT-4 + Zero-shot-CoT with instructor answers and rubrics beats GPT-3.5 and peer grading (score alignment with instructors)
- imaginative/speculative courses (History and Philosophy of Astronomy) hard for LLMs and peer grading
- GPT-4 still closer to instructors than peer grading there

5. Contributions
- (1) explore replacing peer grading with LLMs; automated, more accurate, minimal human involvement, many participants
- (2) 18 scenarios: 2 LLMs x 3 prompting techniques x 3 MOOC topics, real-world data
- (3) GPT-4 + Zero-shot-CoT with instructor answers and rubrics best, incl. vs peer grading; alignment stronger in less creative courses

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
MOOCs (massive open online courses) have changed access to education a lot, because they offer many free courses to anyone who has an internet connection. The platform has democratized education and made it accessible globally, and it can take an unlimited number of participants. But the increase in participant numbers, while it is good for a broader audience, makes it hard to give personalized and constructive feedback on how students perform, and this includes grading their assignments. To deal with this, peer grading has become a common practice. Peer grading increases student engagement and motivation, but people often question its reliability and validity.

The field of Natural Language Processing has gone from applying statistical methods to the recent emergence of large language models (LLMs), and it has fertilized many other disciplines and also made it possible to address more complex tasks. Our methodology is mainly based on a modified version of the zero-shot chain-of-thought prompting (Zero-shot-CoT) technique, where we change the prompt by giving it more in-context understanding of the task.

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
MOOCs (massive open online courses) have changed access to education a lot, because they offer many free courses to anyone who has an internet connection. The platform has democratized education and made it accessible globally, and it can take an unlimited number of participants. But the increase in participant numbers, while it is good for a broader audience, makes it hard to give personalized and constructive feedback on how students perform, and this includes grading their assignments. To deal with this, peer grading has become a common practice. Peer grading increases student engagement and motivation, but people often question its reliability and validity.

The field of Natural Language Processing has gone from applying statistical methods to the recent emergence of large language models (LLMs), and it has fertilized many other disciplines and also made it possible to address more complex tasks. In this study we look at whether LLMs can handle the task of grading assignments in MOOCs and whether it is viable to replace the current peer grading system with LLMs on this platform. The aim is a more streamlined and automated grading mechanism. This could reduce human intervention in grading, so more students can be served with more accurate feedback, and the overall learning experience is improved.

We use three different prompting strategies to assess how well two state-of-the-art LLMs, GPT-4 and GPT-3.5, can grade, in three MOOC subjects: Introductory Astronomy, Astrobiology, and the History and Philosophy of Astronomy. Our methodology is mainly based on a modified version of the zero-shot chain-of-thought prompting (Zero-shot-CoT) technique, where we change the prompt by giving it more in-context understanding of the task. We augment the prompt in three ways: (1) Zero-shot-CoT with instructor-provided answers; (2) Zero-shot-CoT with both instructor-guided answers and grading rubrics; and (3) Zero-shot-CoT with the correct answers from the instructor plus rubrics that the LLM generates based on those correct answers. What we find is that GPT-4 using Zero-shot-CoT prompting with both instructor-provided answers and rubrics does better than GPT-3.5 and peer grading when it comes to how well the scores line up with the instructors' scores. But courses that need imaginative or speculative thinking, such as History and Philosophy of Astronomy, are hard to grade for both LLMs and peer grading. Even so, GPT-4 still does better than peer grading there, with scores closer to the ones the instructors gave.

Our main contributions are:

(1) We look at the potential of replacing peer grading with LLMs in MOOCs, so that grading is automated and more accurate and needs less human involvement, especially when a large number of participants need grading feedback.

(2) We run experiments in 18 different scenarios, using two LLMs (GPT-4 and GPT-3.5) with three prompting techniques (Zero-shot-CoT plus correct answers, Zero-shot-CoT with correct answers and rubrics, and Zero-shot-CoT with correct answers and LLM-presented rubrics) on real-world data from three MOOC topics (Introductory Astronomy, Astrobiology, and the History and Philosophy of Astronomy).

(3) Zero-shot-CoT with correct answers and rubrics written by the instructor, used together with GPT-4, does better than all the other settings, including peer grading, at producing grades that align with the grades given by instructors. However, this alignment is stronger in courses that need less creative and imaginative thinking.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Massive open online courses (MOOCs) have revolutionized access to education by offering a wide range of free courses to anyone with an internet connection. This platform has democratized education and made it globally accessible, accommodating an unlimited number of participants [1,2]. However, the resulting increase in participant numbers, while beneficial to a broader audience, creates challenges in delivering personalized and constructive feedback on student performance, including grading their assignments. To address this issue, peer grading has become common practice. While peer grading enhances student engagement and motivation, its reliability and validity are often questioned [3].

From the application of statistical methods [4,5,6] to the recent emergence of large language models (LLMs), Natural Language Processing has significantly fertilized various other disciplines [7,8,9,10] and has also paved the way for addressing more complex tasks [11]. In this study, we investigate the potential of LLMs for grading assignments in MOOCs and the viability of replacing the current peer grading system with LLMs on this platform, aiming for a more streamlined and automated grading mechanism. This could reduce human intervention in the grading process, thereby serving more students with more accurate feedback and enhancing the overall learning experience.

In this study, we employ three distinct prompting strategies to assess the grading abilities of two state-of-the-art LLMs—GPT-4 [12] and GPT-3.5 [13]—in three MOOC subjects: Introductory Astronomy, Astrobiology, and the History and Philosophy of Astronomy [14,15,16]. Our methodology is primarily based on a modified version of the zero-shot chain-of-thought prompting (Zero-shot-CoT) technique [17], which we tweak by providing more in-context understanding of the given task. In particular, we augment this prompt in three ways: (1) we fortify Zero-shot-CoT with instructor-provided answers; (2) we boost Zero-shot-CoT by integrating both instructor-guided answers and grading rubrics; and (3) we enrich Zero-shot-CoT with correct answers offered by the instructor, supplemented with LLM-generated rubrics based on those answers. Our findings suggest that GPT-4 using Zero-shot-CoT prompting with both instructor-provided answers and rubrics outperforms GPT-3.5 and peer grading in terms of score alignment with the instructors. However, grading courses that require imaginative or speculative thinking, such as History and Philosophy of Astronomy, proves a challenge for both LLMs and peer grading. Even so, GPT-4 still excels over peer grading in such scenarios, producing scores more closely aligned with those given by the instructors.

The main contributions of our study are:

(1) We explore the potential of replacing the peer grading mechanism with LLMs in MOOCs, aiming for an automated and more accurate grading process that minimizes human involvement, particularly when grading feedback is needed for a large number of participants.

(2) Our experiments cover 18 distinct scenarios, applying two LLMs (GPT-4 and GPT-3.5) with three prompting techniques (Zero-shot-CoT plus correct answers, Zero-shot-CoT complemented with correct answers and rubrics, and Zero-shot-CoT with correct answers and LLM-presented rubrics) to real-world data from three MOOC topics (Introductory Astronomy, Astrobiology, and the History and Philosophy of Astronomy).

(3) Integrating Zero-shot-CoT with instructor-crafted correct answers and rubrics, together with GPT-4, outperforms all other settings, including peer grading, in generating grades aligned with those allocated by instructors. However, this alignment is more pronounced in courses that require less creative and imaginative thinking.
